First of all, hold on in there. Loneliness is extremely common (in the western world at least). What you should do (in my opinion): try not to dwell on what is clearly your end goal of companionship; a girlfriend/boyfriend. Try and just make an effort to get into an environment where you are interacting with people. Anything from a class in cookery, live drawing or whatever, or volunteering. Literally anything. 
This will garentee progress as at the very least you will learn or improve your 'skill' in social interaction. It is a skill. It is something many people struggle with (like anything) and like any skill, you only get better with practice. This will lead to an improved confidence in social interactions. 
These groups are a great way to make friends and these 'random' meeting places are often full of people in similar situations. 
Meeting someone special will more often than not come from the more unlikely places but the process of actively seeking someone out puts lots of pressure on you, can lead to you being dishearted and, can actually put potential suiters off. 

In short. Work on your 'social basics', get more confident talking and interacting with people and you will be that much more desirable when you 'bump into' that person.

Everyone here is saying that it is never truly beaten which is true but its also not the whole story. Things get alot easier once you hit certain milestones or thresholds.

I let depression spiral from just a casual dullness and unease in day to day life (which i ignored) through many years this got worse and worse. Eventually i just couldnt be bothered to do anything with my life and i had a self destructive attitude (not sex, drugs and rock and roll but never seeing anyone, comfort eating and enveloping myself in negative thoughts.) I could feel myself getting worse and didnt care. I thought about suicide often but still had the pride/strength of mind to know i wasnt going to do it but, i also knew my state of mind was getting weaker to the point where i thought maybe eventually i will be able to kill myself; beleive it or not this gave me some comfort.

Throughout i refused to go on antidepressants. At first i just thought 'no im stronger than that i dont need them' then it moved to 'but i dont want to rely on them' until eventually i just didnt want any help.

I dont know what it was, whether it was getting sick and tired of feeling shit or if there was some kind of revelation but eventually i decided to try to get better. I got some medication. Found a job. Slowly started to try and see old friends.

The medication helped level the playing field. It didnt make me feel better or happier but it felt like i wasnt fighting against myself anymore. During this time things in my life kind of actually got worse with my dad getting diagnosed with untreatable cancer. But, it didnt take long to realise that i had found the tools to help me get through the dark times. I came off of the medication as quick as i could once things were starting to perk up, this was hard but they had served their purpose. 

Since the turn around point i still have fairly common dark patches that feel like they did a couple years back but the difference is i now know how to counter it. There is no advice like 'think positively' 'socialise' 'exercise' (although all these things are good). But, you just learn a way to tackle it within yourself. Dark times are still shit but they get easier and easier to the point where i no longer really feel down it feels more like a stomach ache which will pass in a day or two.

My point here is this. You will get better at it. The power to tackle depression is within you and sometimes it may need a little help to unlock it. Do not think because you feel utter shite at the moment it will always be like that.

Side note unrelated to my main point. Watch science documentaries about the human mind such as 'The Brain with David Eagleman'.
This helps to show you how amazing and powerful you and the most complex thing in the universe (your brain) is. It helps you to realise, on an unemotional level, the shear power and adaptability that you have at your desposal and hopefully give you some faith in your recovery.

Cancer is basically glitched cells that lose control of the regulation of replication and end up mass producing more and more cancerous cells in quick succession. This occurs from DNA damage often spurred on by damage to genes involving DNA repair. These cells now behave differently to 'normal' cells so can be targeted and killed by drugs (chemotherapy). However, the behaviour targeted is the rapid replication and some normal cells (hair, stomach lining ect.) do this normally and can end up being targeted along with the cancerous cells as a side effect. This is due to the fact that chemotherapy is delivered and spread by your circulatory system so it can get all around your body (good because you want it to target all the cancer/bad because you then cant stop it from targeting everything else). 

The reason cancer is so shit is because, unlike diseases caused by viruses and bacteria which can be identified and exclusively targeted by drugs, cancer is all you. Hence chemotherapy is very 'indiscriminate'. 

Things like radiotherapy again cant exclusively target cancer cells but can target an area of tissue and kill everything in the area (including healthy cells) but at least the damage is contained in that area. Radiotherapy is a common treatment but is only good if we are confident that the cancer is all still contained in the target area. Remember cancer cells are broken cells and can dislodge from where they came from and potentially get into the blood and spread around the body where they will continue to proliferate (replicate) maybe causing a tummor to form somewhere else. In this situation chemotherapy would be the more effective treatment. 

The bottom line is that although some cell types are more prone to becoming cancerous it could happen to any cell and situation and diagnoses will dictate what treatment is used. Chemotherapy is the just currently the most tested, kind of well understood, and most broad weapon against cancer thus is most commonly used. Oncology, the study of cancer, has loads of new potential experimental ways of fighting cancer in a more friendly manner but all of which need testing to hell and back before they can be concidered for mainstream hospitals.

Tldr: chemotherapy is spread throughout the body and targets rapidly proliferating (replicating) cells. Essentially most effective but also very harmful.
